title: Design a Run Cursor
statement_md:
A sensor logs one integer reading per tick and hands them over as a **stream**: a
one-pass sequence you can only read forwards. You may ask whether any reading is
left, and take the next one, but you can't rewind, look ahead, or ask how long it
is. Consecutive equal readings form a **run**: `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1]` has the runs
`1×2`, `2×3` and `1×1` (the last `1` is a new run, because a `2` came between).

Implement `RunCursor`, which walks the stream's runs one at a time. A run is
reported as the two-element list `[value, length]`:

- `RunCursor(nums)` wraps the stream `nums`, positioned before the first run.
- `next()` returns the next run and moves past it, or `[]` if no run is left.
- `peek()` returns what `next()` would, without moving. `[]` if no run is left.
- `hasNext()` returns whether a run is left.
- `skip(k)` moves past up to `k` runs and returns how many it actually moved
  past, which is less than `k` only when the stream ran out. `skip(0)` does nothing.

Every call must agree with the runs of the *whole* stream, however the calls are
interleaved. In particular a run's length is only known once its last reading has
been seen, and a stream can't be un-read.

**Complexity.** Every reading may be taken from the stream at most once, and all
calls together must run in $O(n)$ time for a stream of $n$ readings. The cursor
**must** hold only $O(1)$ memory of its own: it processes the stream as it goes
rather than copying it.

languages.note_md: `nums` is the harness's `Iterator`: `nums.hasNext()` says whether a reading is left and `nums.next()` takes it. `RunCursor` returns plain lists.

`nums` is an `IntIter`, a standard `Iterator<Item = i32>` (so `nums.next()` returns an `Option<i32>`, and `nums.len()` is how many readings are left). `next` and `peek` return `Vec<i32>`, with an empty vector for `[]`. `hasNext` is called as `has_next`.

constraints: At most $10^4$ calls will be made to `next`, `peek`, `hasNext` and `skip`.

solutions.title: Drain the Stream Up Front
solutions.intuition_md:
Every question the cursor answers is about the list of *runs*, not about the
stream. So the direct approach is to produce that list once: read the stream to
the end, merging each reading into the last run if it's equal to that run's value
and starting a new run otherwise. After that the cursor is an index into a list.

`next`, `peek` and `hasNext` are list reads, and `skip(k)` is a clamped index bump.
Nothing about *when* a run ends is left to think about, because the whole stream
has already been seen.

It passes every case, but it breaks the requirement above. It copies the stream
into memory, $O(n)$ of it, and it reads the entire stream before the first call
returns, even if the caller only wanted one run. A stream too long to hold, or one
that's produced slowly, is exactly the case a cursor exists for.
solutions.algorithm_md:
1. In the constructor, read every reading `x` from the stream. If the last run's
   value is `x`, add 1 to its length, otherwise append `[x, 1]`. Set `i = 0`.
2. `next()`: if `i` is past the end, return `[]`; otherwise return `runs[i]` and
   increment `i`. `peek()` is the same without the increment.
3. `hasNext()`: `i < len(runs)`.
4. `skip(k)`: let `n = min(k, len(runs) - i)`, add `n` to `i`, return `n`.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: The constructor reads each reading once; every later call is $O(1)$.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: All the runs are stored, up to $n$ of them when no two neighbours are equal. This is the solution the memory requirement rules out.

solutions.title: Read One Run Ahead
solutions.intuition_md:
A cursor only ever needs the *next* run, so it can read the stream a run at a time.
The catch is that a run doesn't announce its end: the only way to know that a run of
`2`s is over is to read the next value and find it isn't a `2`. And that value has
been taken off the stream for good. Dropping it would lose the first reading of the
following run, and there's no way to put it back.

So the cursor keeps exactly two things beyond the stream itself. `buf` is the run
it has read but not yet handed out, which is what makes `peek` free to call twice
and `next` after a `peek` agree with it. `carry` is the one reading it had to read
past the end of that run, which becomes the start of the next run when it's needed.
Both are a couple of numbers, so memory stays $O(1)$, and the stream is consumed
lazily: a run is read only when a call needs it.

The subtle case is `hasNext`. Once `carry` holds a reading, the stream itself may
already report nothing left, yet a run remains. So `hasNext` has to ask all three:
the buffered run, the carried reading, and the stream.
solutions.algorithm_md:
1. State: the `stream`, `buf` (a run or nothing) and `carry` (a reading or nothing).
2. `load()`: if `buf` is set, stop. Otherwise take the run's first reading from
   `carry` (clearing it) or from the stream, and stop if neither has one. Then read
   while the stream has readings equal to it, counting them. On the first reading
   that differs, store it in `carry` and stop reading. Set `buf = [value, count]`.
3. `peek()`: `load()`, then return `buf` (or `[]`). `next()`: the same, but clear `buf`.
4. `hasNext()`: `buf` is set, or `carry` is set, or the stream has a reading left.
5. `skip(k)`: repeat up to `k` times: `load()`, stop if `buf` is empty, clear `buf`,
   and count it. Return the count.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Each reading is taken from the stream once, either into a run's count or into `carry`, so all calls together do $O(n)$ work.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Only the buffered run and one carried reading are held, whatever the length of the stream.
